item.title: DiJonai Carrington hits two players across the face, receives technical foul after Sophie Cunningham drama
item.description: DiJonai Carrington hit three players in the face in four days, including Sophie Cunningham's bloody mouth foul and two hits against Golden State.
item.content:encoded:
Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington swears that she isn't a dirty player, but her actions on the court aren't exactly helping that narrative.

Carrington made major headlines last week by committing a very hard foul on Sophie Cunningham during a layup attempt that left the Indiana Fever star with a bloody mouth. Carrington was ejected from the contest after the foul was determined to be a Flagrant 2, and shortly after being tossed from the contest, posted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" on her Instagram Threads account, insinuating skin color played a role in the decision.

Fast-forward just four days after the foul and controversy involving Cunningham, and Carrington was back on the floor making contact with players' faces.

CLUELESS WNBA ATTACKS 'BAD-FAITH' FANS WHO DON'T WANT BIOLOGICAL MEN RUINING WOMEN'S SPORTS

During Chicago's 91-71 loss to the Golden State Valkyries on Wednesday, Carrington was guarding Cecilia Zandalasini on the perimeter, and while swiping at the ball, caught the Golden State forward in the eye.

The hand movement from Carrington on the play was odd. While she was clearly using her right hand to attack the ball, her left hand was in a position where it was physically impossible for her to reach the ball unless it went through Zandalasini's face.

Players being poked in the eye or catching a finger across the face while being closely defended is a typical play in basketball, but the same can't be said for Carrington's second above-the-neck hit against Golden State.

As Tiffany Hayes made a mid-air move on a layup attempt, Carrington jumped with her and threw her arm down, failing to hit the basketball, and instead caught the Valkyries' guard in the mouth.

Neither of Carrington's fouls to the face against Golden State resulted in flagrant or technical fouls, but she did pick up what was her second technical of the season for arguing with a referee during the third quarter.

With Carrington now hitting three separate players in the face in just a four-day stretch, it's worth revisiting the message she posted on X during the 2025 season about not being a dirty player.

"Yall fAnS swear i’m such a dirty player. I’m SO over this narrative bc if u really know bball, u know I jus play hard asf & never give up on a play," Carrington wrote in June 2025. "&yup, we challenged the last couple flagrants & got em rescinded bc I’m ALWAYS tryna make a play on the ball nun more, nun less."

Carrington did not receive any form of repercussions for her Flagrant 2 foul on Cunningham or for posting "WHITE PRIVILEGE" on social media. The WNBA did not address the situation publicly and did not issue a comment to OutKick upon multiple requests.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON’T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

According to Carrington, folks who assumed that her post about white privilege played a role in the foul on Cunningham or her ejection had it all wrong.

"I’ve never once claimed that the assessment of the foul was white privilege (that was your assumption)," Cunningam wrote on X, two days after her hard foul on Cunningham.

"Furthermore, I’m the LAST thing from ignorant or asinine when it comes to speaking on 'white privilege,' do ya research on that one," she continued. "I actually went to school, one of the top universities might I add, to educate myself on this exact subject," Carrington, who attended Stanford for four years before grad-transferring to Baylor, added. "I would never use that term as a rhetorical weapon knowing the historical and social weight it holds without having the proper evidence to substantiate it."

Cunningham came off the bench for Chicago against Golden State on Wednesday, scoring three points while shooting 1-for-9 from the floor in 24 minutes of action.

item.title: ‘X-Men’ star Tyler Mane says wife ‘saved my life’ after seemingly harmless lump led to breast cancer diagnosis
item.description: Tyler Mane credits his wife Renae with saving his life after she insisted he get a breast lump checked that turned out to be Stage 1 cancer. They're now co-hosting a new podcast, "Mane AF."
item.content:encoded:
Tyler Mane, who was recently diagnosed with breast cancer, believes his wife may have saved his life.

The actor is teaming up with his wife, Renae, for a candid new podcast, "Mane AF," tackling the realities of "midlife, marriage and mayhem." The couple will also open up about one of their most personal challenges yet: navigating his diagnosis of invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC).

Mane made his feature-film debut as Sabretooth in 2000's "X-Men" and later reprised the role as Wolverine's nemesis in 2024's "Deadpool & Wolverine." He also starred as Michael Myers in 2007's "Halloween" and 2009's "Halloween II," and appeared as Ajax in 2004's "Troy."

FORMER WRESTLER, ACTOR REVEALS BREAST CANCER DIAGNOSIS: 'ONE IN 750 MEN'

"She just kept insisting," the former wrestler told Fox News Digital about seeing a doctor. "I kept talking about it, 'I have this lump here still, and it's hard.' And she was very insistent because women are trained from a certain age that if they feel something in their breast area, go get it checked out."

"I have to thank her," he said. "She saved my life by saying, 'Get in there and get tested.'"

When the 59-year-old first noticed a lump in his breast area, he assumed it was a lipoma — a soft, fatty growth he'd had removed before. But this lump felt different. Mane initially brushed it off, but Renae kept urging him, "Go in and get checked." Eventually, he listened.

WATCH: TYLER MANE SAYS WIFE ‘SAVED MY LIFE’ AFTER CANCER DIAGNOSIS

"To be honest, even my doctor said, 'Oh, it's probably nothing. It's probably just a lipoma,'" Mane recalled. "And then, when I went in for the [surgery], he said, 'You probably want to get that removed, but it's probably nothing.' It's just dismissed so much that you have to be an advocate for your own body. And I'm just so thankful that she was an advocate for my body. Otherwise, it could have been a whole different story."

Mane said a 28-millimeter tumor was removed.

"It was removed, I think, on a Thursday," Mane said. "I went on a trip and thought nothing of it. I came back, got up and started working at 6am, and then I got the news: invasive ductal carcinoma. I went and woke my wife up. She's like, 'This is not good.' She was half-asleep but woke up very quickly. And that's when our journey began."

Because breast cancer is predominantly associated with women, many men are unaware that they are also at risk. The American Cancer Society estimates that in 2026, about 2,670 men in the U.S. will be diagnosed with invasive breast cancer and about 530 will die from the disease.

According to the American Cancer Society, the average lifetime risk of breast cancer for men is about 1 in 755.

The most common symptom of male breast cancer is a firm, usually painless lump under or near the nipple, according to experts. Other signs can include skin dimpling, nipple retraction and nipple discharge. Mane said the lump was the only symptom he experienced before his diagnosis.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Male breast cancer is rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of breast cancers in the U.S. Screening mammograms are not usually recommended for men, even those at increased risk, according to the National Cancer Institute.

"This is a cancer that anyone can get," Mane said. "If you feel something different in your chest than the norm, you have to go get it checked out and tested. You have to insist on getting tested and checked. You have to be the best advocate for yourself."

"For sure, I wanted to keep my diagnosis private at the beginning because I felt a bit ashamed," Mane admitted. "I was like, 'How can I have breast cancer?' But then I quickly turned to, 'No, I got to talk about this because this is a very serious issue that men don't usually deal with.'"

While male breast cancer can occur at any age, the risk increases with age, according to the American Cancer Society. Treatment usually starts with surgery, while other common treatments include chemotherapy, hormone therapy and radiation therapy, according to Mayo Clinic. Treatment depends on factors including the cancer's stage and the patient's overall health.

"I was a Stage 1, so we got it early," Mane said. "Now we're into the chemotherapy ... to make sure that it's completely out of my system ... and then after the chemotherapy, I have some radiation to make sure we hit that area specifically."

For Mane, some days are easier than others.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"Chemotherapy is hard on your system," he said. "Unless you've gone through it, you can't even imagine what it does to your body, and it's a repetitive cycle. It's not like you get an injury, and you rehabilitate it, or like when I had my hips replaced, and it's one and done. With chemotherapy, it's ongoing. You have your chemo treatment, where they put all of the chemicals into you."

"You feel like c--- for about the first week, and then you have a couple of weeks where you're like, 'I'm just getting back to normal now,'" he continued. "And then you have to go in, sit in that chair again and have that pumped into your body again to kill off the cancer cells. It's about the hardest thing to psych yourself up for."

"Right now, I want to take a nap, but I've got the metal mouth. And that's one thing: every round I've had something different thrown at me. I couldn't lift my shoulder over my head. One time I broke out in hives. But it's just your body trying to kick it out and get ready for the next round."

Known for playing some of Hollywood's most intimidating characters, Mane said he's bringing that same fighting spirit to his cancer treatment, with Renae by his side every step of the way.

"I knew I had it in me," he said with a smile. "You have to have a positive attitude, and I've stayed positive no matter what. You have to stay positive. As soon as you let yourself get down, then it's a downhill slide from there. And I need to stick around for my wife and my family. It's time to step up and do what I have to do."

As Mane continues to talk publicly about his diagnosis, he hopes to use the podcast to raise awareness about breast cancer in men, including by bringing his oncologist on as a guest. But he wants other men to take another lesson from his experience to heart: listen to your wife. She just might save your life.

"All you guys out there, listen to your wives when they tell you to get checked," he said.

Fox News Digital’s Khloe Quill contributed to this report.

item.title: California law puts digital fingerprints on AI fakes
item.description: The California AI Transparency Act now requires hidden provenance data in AI-generated images, video and audio, but these digital fingerprints have limits.
item.content:encoded:
California now wants artificial intelligence-made images, videos and recordings to carry a traceable history. The California AI Transparency Act took effect Aug. 2. It requires large generative AI providers to embed hidden provenance information in covered media created by their systems.

That means a suspicious recording may carry clues about which AI system produced it and when. You will no longer have to rely only on how convincing it looks or sounds. Still, these digital fingerprints come with limits. They can reveal details about a file's history, but they cannot determine whether the message inside it is true.

The law also adds requirements for large online platforms beginning in 2027. Newly produced phones, cameras and voice recorders face another set of rules in 2028. Here is how the system will work, where it may fall short and why other states could soon follow California's lead.

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

IS CYBERBULLYING HIDING IN YOUR CHILD'S GROUP CHAT?

California enacted the original AI Transparency Act in 2024. State Sen. Josh Becker authored the legislation, known as SB 942. Lawmakers later expanded its reach through AB 853. The law applies to companies that create generative AI systems with more than 1 million monthly visitors or users. Those systems must also be publicly accessible in California.

California calls these companies "covered providers." They must include a hidden disclosure in AI-generated images, video and audio created by their systems. The law calls this a latent disclosure. When technically feasible and reasonable, the disclosure must convey the provider's name, the name and version of the AI system, the date and time the content was created or altered and a unique identifier.

The disclosure must follow widely accepted industry standards. It must also remain permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove when technically feasible. The law focuses these hidden disclosure requirements on images, video and audio. It does not require the same embedded disclosure in AI-generated text. Covered providers must also offer users the option to add a visible AI label. That notice must clearly identify the content as AI-generated.

Covered AI providers must offer a detection tool at no cost. The tool must let you upload an image, video or audio file. You can also submit a link to content stored online. It then checks whether that provider's own AI system created or altered the material. The tool must display any system provenance information it finds.

However, a detection tool from one AI company may not identify media produced by another company. Therefore, a negative result does not prove that a human created the content. The law also places privacy limits on these tools. Providers generally cannot collect personal information from users. They cannot keep submitted content longer than necessary either. A violation can bring a $5,000 civil penalty. Each day of noncompliance can count as a separate violation for covered providers, large platforms and device manufacturers.

Provenance data acts like a history attached to a digital file. It may identify the system that produced the content. It can also record when someone created or changed the file.

The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity, commonly called C2PA, has developed an open technical standard for this purpose. Its Content Credentials system can preserve information about a file's source and editing history. For example, someone may send you an audio recording that appears to feature a public official. A compatible verification tool could reveal that an AI system generated the recording.

That information might stop you from sharing the clip too quickly. It could also help expose a scammer using a cloned voice. However, provenance data does not judge whether a statement is accurate. C2PA says its system provides evidence about a file's origin and history, but that information alone cannot prove the content is truthful. A real photograph can still appear beside a false caption. Someone can also edit authentic footage to remove important context.

TOP MEDIA OUTLETS FAIL TO DISCLOSE WHO IS BANKROLLING THEIR AI REPORTERS

The next major phase starts Jan. 1, 2027. Large online platforms will have to detect compatible provenance data embedded in content they distribute. The law covers public-facing social media services and file-sharing platforms. It also includes qualifying mass messaging services and stand-alone search engines. A service falls under this section if it exceeded 2 million unique monthly users during the previous 12 months.

Covered platforms must tell users when system provenance data is available. They must also show the name of the AI system or capture device connected to the file, when applicable. In addition, the platform must indicate whether digital signatures are available. Users must have an accessible way to inspect the information. A platform can display the data directly or let the user download a copy that retains it. The platform can also send the user to a separate verification service.

Finally, platforms cannot knowingly strip compatible system provenance data or digital signatures when preserving them is technically feasible. This phase could bring the most noticeable change for everyday users. Most people will not visit a separate verification website for every questionable post. A notice built into a social platform could make checking suspicious content much easier.

Another phase begins Jan. 1, 2028. It covers recording devices first produced for sale in California on or after that date. This includes mobile phones with built-in cameras or microphones. Traditional cameras and voice recorders also fall under the definition. Manufacturers must give users the option to include a hidden disclosure in captured content. They must also embed the disclosure by default when doing so is technically feasible.

The information can include the manufacturer and device model. It may also record the date and time when the device created or altered the content. That could establish a starting point for authentic media. For example, the credential may show that an image began as a photograph captured by a real camera. Later information could reveal whether compatible editing software altered it. Still, the requirement will not update every phone or camera already in use. It applies to covered devices first produced for sale in California beginning in 2028.

Artificial intelligence can produce realistic voices and convincing video faster than lawmakers can update most regulations. Cybercriminals can now fake faces and voices in real time. As CyberGuy previously reported, AI deepfake scams can impersonate trusted executives during live video calls. One documented attack convinced an employee to transfer millions of dollars.

Scammers can also imitate someone you love. An AI voice scam can clone a family member from only a few seconds of public audio. Personal information found online can make the fake emergency even more convincing. California lawmakers have also raised concerns about election misinformation and abusive deepfakes. Generative AI can create fake political audio or video that appears to show a candidate saying something that never happened. It can also help bad actors produce false social media posts quickly. CyberGuy has previously examined how AI and other technology can fuel election-related scams, including deepfake videos and fabricated news.

Federal lawmakers are responding too. Sen. Adam Schiff and Rep. Ro Khanna reintroduced the AI Ads Act on July 27. The proposal would prohibit fraudulent misrepresentation of political candidates or committees through AI-generated content. However, it has not become federal law. A separate bipartisan proposal called the AI Labeling Act was introduced on June 24. It would require visible and machine-readable disclosures on covered AI-generated content. That bill would also require major social platforms and AI developers to work together on authenticity tools. It has not become law either. California's system places identifying information inside compatible files. That data may continue traveling with the content as people download or repost it. However, that protection depends on websites and editing tools preserving the credentials.

BABYLON BEE SUES NEW MEXICO OFFICIALS OVER LAW REQUIRING AI DISCLAIMERS ON POLITICAL SATIRE

Yes, other states are likely to move in the same direction. However, they may not copy California's entire system. Many states already regulate AI-generated political content. Their laws often require a visible disclaimer or restrict deceptive deepfakes near an election. Colorado goes further by requiring metadata in certain political deepfakes. That metadata must identify the tool used and when the content was created. Utah requires tamper-evident digital provenance for some synthetic political media. Its rules can identify who created the content and whether other parties changed it.

Louisiana added disclosure requirements in 2026 for AI-generated telephone campaign communications, including calls that use the voice of a public figure. Other states have chosen narrower rules focused on specific election periods. California's law reaches beyond campaign advertising. It places requirements on major AI providers now, followed by large platforms and newly produced recording devices. The European Union is moving in a similar direction. Article 50 of the EU AI Act became applicable on Aug. 2. Covered AI providers must add machine-readable marks that allow people to detect generated or manipulated content. Deployers also face disclosure requirements for deepfakes.

That overlap may push large technology companies toward broader adoption. A company may find it easier to use one provenance system across its products than to maintain a special version for California. As a result, people nationwide could see some benefits before their own state passes a similar law. Still, that outcome isn’t guaranteed. Enforcement will matter, along with whether popular platforms preserve and clearly display the information.

The new law creates a helpful signal, but several gaps remain. First, missing provenance data does not prove that a human created the file. The media may come from an AI provider that falls below California's size threshold. It could also have been generated before the law became operative. In addition, some editing programs may fail to preserve the information. A scammer could play an AI-generated video on one device and record it with another. That new recording might not retain the original credentials.

Screenshots can also lose embedded information. The same problem may affect compressed copies shared through messaging services. C2PA notes that provenance records can be incomplete. It also warns that a file without Content Credentials should not automatically be treated as untrustworthy. Most importantly, a valid credential does not certify that the message is true. You still need to consider who posted the content and whether another reliable source confirms the claim.

The California AI transparency law gives you another tool when a recording or image feels suspicious. Look for a Content Credentials icon or another provenance notice when a platform displays one. When possible, inspect the original file instead of relying on a screenshot. You can also use a detection tool offered by the AI provider. However, remember that the tool may recognize only content created by that company's system. For messages involving money, contact the person or business through a number you already trust. Do not use contact information included with the suspicious content.

For a claimed political statement, check the official account or website connected to the person shown. Then look for independent reporting from a credible source. Also, watch for pressure to react immediately. Urgency can keep you from noticing that a voice sounds slightly wrong or a video contains visual glitches. For more warning signs, CyberGuy's article on how to spot and stop AI phishing scams explains how to check suspicious messages, voice clones and deepfake video. Finally, do not treat the absence of an AI label as proof that something is real.

California's AI transparency law gives you a practical way to investigate synthetic media. Hidden provenance information may reveal which AI system created a file and when that happened. The platform requirements could have an even greater effect. A built-in notice is easier to use than expecting everyone to locate a separate verification website. Still, digital fingerprints will not eliminate deception. Scammers will look for tools outside the law's reach. Older media will also continue circulating without credentials. California is now testing whether transparency can restore some trust in digital content. Other states are already taking related steps and more are likely to follow.

If an AI-generated recording can influence an election or empty someone's bank account before anyone checks it, should every state require a traceable digital identity? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: JD Vance calls on DOJ to prosecute alleged fraud in teen transgender treatment
item.description: JD Vance refers a bombshell HHS report to the Justice Department alleging hospitals pushed gender affirming care on minors to boost profits.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Vice President JD Vance is calling for the Department of Justice to investigate a bombshell Health and Human Services (HHS) report alleging some hospitals and healthcare providers fraudulently subjected children to lucrative sex-change procedures.

The new report, titled: "Wolves in White Coats: How Doctors and Hospitals Pushed and Profited from the Fraud of 'Gender Medicine,'" revealed more than $60 million in insurance claims for treatments including puberty blockers for adolescents as young as 13 billed from 2015 to 2025.

According to HHS, some providers aggressively treated children who presented with hormonal issues, endocrine system problems, or early onset puberty with transgender care, billing insurance companies. HHS also blamed Biden-era policies promoting transgender treatments for expanding access gender surgery coverage.

MEDICAID ENDS FUNDING FOR CHILD SEX-CHANGE PROCEDURES AS TRUMP ADMIN SLAMS 'EXPERIMENTAL' TREATMENTS

Fox News Digital obtained a letter from Vance to Attorney General Todd Blanche which detailed Vance’s concerns surrounding the report, and called for criminal prosecution of anyone who has intentionally misled children to get transgender treatment.

"One study showed that only about 4.7 percent of patients diagnosed with "endocrine disorder, unspecified," had that actual condition," Vance wrote in the letter to Blanche. "Another notes a 30 percent increase in the number of endocrine disorder diagnoses, despite it being unlikely that that there has been a substantial increase in pediatric endocrine disorders."

The average healthcare cost for a minor is roughly $3,000, but transgender treatments can push that to $75,000 without surgery and nearly $170,000, if surgery is involved, according to the report.

The report also details how some healthcare providers profit from life-long medical costs, including prescriptions, surgeries and medical interventions years after a minor reaches adulthood.

About 225 hospitals and health systems across the country have established pediatric gender programs. Vance charged in his letter to Blanche that health care providers knowingly pushed their misdiagnoses to insurance companies, using billing codes to compel coverage.

VANCE REFERS TIM WALZ, MINNESOTA ATTORNEY GENERAL TO DOJ FOR CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION OVER STATE'S ALLEGED FRAUD

"When providers miscode treatment in order to secure insurance coverage for gender-transitioning interventions that insurance would not otherwise cover, they should be held accountable," read Vance’s letter. "If they have done so intentionally, thereby perpetrating a fraud on Medicaid or on private insurers, they should go to prison."

"Rather than allow the proliferation of harmful, sex-rejecting procedures on our children, we must send a clear message that any hospitals and providers that have participated in these practices will face justice."

The HHS report cited peer-reviewed scientific literature, hospital records, whistleblower testimony, nationwide insurance claims analyses and interviews with patients and parents.

Hours after President Joe Biden was sworn into office in 2021, he signed Executive Order 13988, titled: "Preventing and Combating Discrimination on the Basis of Gender Identity or Sexual Orientation."

COLORADO SUPREME COURT ORDERS CHILDREN'S HOSPITAL TO RESUME GENDER TRANSITION TREATMENTS FOR MINORS

"Children should be able to learn without worrying about whether they will be denied access to the restroom, the locker room, or school sports," the executive order read. "People should be able to access healthcare and secure a roof over their heads without being subjected to sex discrimination."

The executive order’s mandate took effect, and in May of 2021, Biden’s HHS said its Office of Civil Rights would enforce an Affordable Care Act nondiscrimination provision, which includes sex discrimination.

In a March 2022 notice, the department "unequivocally" confirmed "that gender affirming care for minors, when medically appropriate and necessary, improves their physical and mental health."

In a separate executive order signed by Biden in June of 2022, Biden directed the federal government, including his HHS, to "address the discrimination and barriers that LGBTQI+ individuals and families face by expanding access to comprehensive health care."

LARGEST CHILDREN’S HOSPITAL IN US TO OPEN ‘DETRANSITION CLINIC’ AFTER $10M SETTLEMENT WITH TRUMP DOJ, STATE

Fox News Digital also obtained a letter from HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. to HHS Inspector General Thomas March Bell that included a sizable list of individual hospitals and clinicians that Kennedy says exhibit "potentially anomalous billing patterns."

The report calls for additional review of insurance coding practices that enable hospitals and clinicians to file claims for gender medicine.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department but did not receive a response in time for publication.

item.title: Jayden Daniels tells LSU to keep his name out of its mouth in wild No. 5 jersey feud involving NIL
item.description: Lane Kiffin says D.J. Pickett was promised the No. 5 jersey during recruiting, but Jayden Daniels and his family feel profoundly disrespected by LSU.
item.content:encoded:
Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels has decided to start a legal war with his former school, LSU, over the rights to his name, image and likeness — and it all stems from the use of his former college jersey number.

Yes, the Heisman Trophy winner is trying to distance himself from the LSU football program and prevent the school from using promotional material related to his time in Baton Rouge.

Why?

Because LSU is allowing current cornerback D.J. Pickett to wear the No. 5 jersey this upcoming season, a number Daniels believes should not be worn due to what he accomplished during his time on the Bayou.

Earlier this month, an attorney representing Daniels sent a cease-and-desist letter to the LSU athletic department detailing a list of demands regarding the school's use of Daniels' NIL.

In the letter, first reported by ESPN and confirmed by Fox News Digital-OutKick, attorney Adam Kenner was very specific about what he expects from LSU moving forward.

"Accordingly, LSU must immediately cease and desist from any further issue use, display, publication, distribution, promotion, commercialization, or other exploitation of Mr. Daniels' NIL in any manner or medium," Kenner detailed in a letter to AD Verge Ausberry. "Any use of Mr. Daniels' NIL occurring after LSU's receipt of this notice will be deemed knowing and willful and will be pursued vigorously through all available legal and equitable remedies, without further notice."

I think it's pretty easy to tell that this kerfuffle is not going away any time soon.

After Daniels won the 2023 Heisman Trophy, the clock started ticking on when LSU could potentially retire his jersey number. Under LSU's policy, there is a five-year waiting period before that discussion can take place.

But that doesn't mean LSU can't allow another player to wear the number in the meantime. According to the athletic department's protocol, that decision comes down to the head coach's discretion.

Legendary halfback Billy Cannon, who wore No. 20 while playing at LSU, had his number permanently retired, meaning it cannot be worn again. Other legendary Tigers have had their jerseys retired while their numbers remain available for current players.

So, with the clock still ticking on when LSU can even discuss retiring the No. 5 that Daniels wore after transferring in from Arizona State, former head coach Brian Kelly told ESPN that he promised the number to current cornerback D.J. Pickett during the recruiting process.

Yes, I promise you, this is a thing in college athletics — and has been for years. If a school is heavily recruiting an athlete who wants to wear a certain number, the program can promise that number as part of the recruiting process to entice an athlete to sign.

But Daniels was apparently under the impression that LSU should have asked him beforehand whether he was OK with another player wearing No. 5 for the first time since he left Baton Rouge for the NFL.

It should also be noted that Joe Burrow, who won the 2019 Heisman Trophy and led LSU to a national championship, has not had his No. 9 worn by another player in Baton Rouge since leaving for the NFL.

So, is Daniels upset that his number is being handed to another player while Burrow's has remained untouched?

That's likely part of the equation, especially given the statement provided by a spokesperson for Daniels.

"The Daniels family is deeply disappointed and feels profoundly disrespected by LSU's decision to give Jayden's number to another player," Jayden Daniels' spokesperson said. "Jayden and his family had every reason to believe that his number would remain a meaningful part of his LSU legacy and would be honored and protected in recognition of his extraordinary contributions to the university."

It appears Daniels is upset that, while former coach Brian Kelly held off on allowing someone else to wear the number, current head coach Lane Kiffin is honoring a promise made to a player during the previous regime's time in Baton Rouge.

This is obviously a no-win situation for the LSU head coach.

Either he's going to accommodate DJ Pickett or upset former Heisman Trophy quarterback Jayden Daniels.

LANE KIFFIN KNOWS THERE AREN’T EXCUSES AT LSU. NOW COMES THE TEST OF MAKING IT WORTH THE PRICE OF ADMISSION

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

When asked about the situation during a recent news conference at LSU, Lane Kiffin was adamant that he's simply keeping a promise the previous staff made to Pickett.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

"DJ is in No.5, and that was a situation that was promised to him in recruiting here, for him to sign here," Kiffin told reporters. "I've done a lot of research on that with the family and the representatives and the people, so really I didn't have a decision to make. It was promised to the kid. It wasn't done for whatever reason. I'm not going to get into that.

"I'm not going to judge something [that was done] when I wasn't here. But when a kid is promised something to come to a school, he should wear it. So at that point, I don't think that's really my decision. We should honor what he was told."

So, this ultimately comes down to a former player who feels disrespected by his old school and a current head coach caught in the middle of an increasingly messy dispute between Daniels and LSU administrators.

item.title: Wisconsin Democratic candidate for governor David Crowley reveals he won't campaign with Hasan Piker
item.description: David Crowley said he won't campaign with Hasan Piker, distancing himself from platforms he says divide the Democratic Party ahead of the Wisconsin governor's race.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate David Crowley said he would not be campaigning with far-left socialist Twitch streamer Hasan Piker during an interview released on Wednesday.

Crowley said he didn't want to lend credibility to platforms that further divide the Democratic Party, in an interview with WISN 12 News.

"I don’t want to lend credibility to platforms, if you will, that I believe further divide us as a community, further divide Democrats, or further divide this country. But, I do know that we have to focus on bringing everybody under this tent," Crowley said.

MEET THE DEMOCRAT WHO NARROWLY DEFEATED SOCIALIST RIVAL IN KEY SWING-STATE BATTLE OVER THE PARTY’S FUTURE

"So, I’m always willing to have those tough conversations. But we also have to utilize not just myself —there are many community members, there are many voters, there are many supporters that we can empower to bring people to be a part of this big tent we call the Democratic Party," he said.

WISN 12 News' Matt Smith asked Crowley directly if he was talking about Piker specifically, and if he was planning to campaign with the streamer.

"I’m talking about anybody who focuses on divisive language," he said, adding, "I don’t plan on campaigning with Hasan, if that’s what you’re asking me. No."

Piker campaigned alongside Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist who ran against Crowley in the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary.

HASAN PIKER CALLS FOR DEMOCRATS WHO OPPOSE ABDUL EL-SAYED TO BE 'PUNISHED'

The streamer reacted to Crowley's remarks on X.

"this is devastating news for me, i however wish crowley the best of luck for the wisconsin trifecta. hope he takes some of the great policies that brought out 300k wisconsinites into consideration as the dems work to defeat tom tiffany as a unified front!" Piker wrote.

Piker said Wednesday that "the knives will be out" for the socialist left after Hong's loss in the Wisconsin primary.

Piker argued during his livestream that Democratic establishment figures will work harder to stop insurgent candidates because they no longer underestimate the progressive movement.

"It will be more difficult, though, because the establishment will not underestimate us. It will continue to undermine us, but they will not underestimate us," Piker said. "So, the knives will be out."

Eric Ham, a political analyst, told Fox News Digital in a statement that Crowley's comments "fuel division within the Democratic Party and only makes it harder for the party to be a viable check on the Trump administration.

"Moreover, as the economy falters and the war in Iran grows more unpopular, Democrats have a very real shot at tangible pickups, not just in Washington, but in state and local races. Wisconsin is a clear example of this. Now is the time for the party, left and center, to unify behind its candidates and chart clear messaging and contrasts versus Republicans. Otherwise, Democrats risk squandering tremendous gains in November," Ham continued.

The Democratic Socialists of America did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: House Republican urges new Trump AG Blanche to shut down Biden-era NYC heroin injection sites
item.description: Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding swift action to shut down OnPoint's overdose prevention centers in Manhattan.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., slammed Biden administration-funded heroin injection sites in New York City in an interview with Fox News Digital.

At the heart of Malliotakis' complaints are two Overdose Prevention Centers (OPCs) in Manhattan — one in East Harlem and the other in Washington Heights — that, until recently, funneled federal funds to "supervised consumption services," including the supervised use of illicit drugs such as heroin, a Schedule I controlled substance.

"People literally go there like it's a community center, hang out, and shoot up drugs. It's signaling to drug dealers where their clients are located and attracting a criminal element in and around the facility," Malliotakis told Fox News Digital.

"We don't want to see this spread throughout the City of New York or the rest of the country, which is why it's critical for the Department of Justice to step in now to stop these illegally operating heroin injection centers — to make an example of what's taking place in New York City so other municipalities throughout the country don't think about opening them," she continued.

EX-EMPLOYEE OF TAXPAYER-FUNDED NONPROFIT CAUGHT SELLING FENTANYL NEAR LA PARK: DOCS

Malliotakis wrote a letter to newly-confirmed U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche on Tuesday, requesting that he take "swift action" to shut down the centers.

She accused the nonprofit OnPoint, which runs the centers, of "operating in clear violation of federal law under Title 21 of the United States Code Section 856 which states it is unlawful to '...knowingly open, lease, rent, use, or maintain any place, whether permanently or temporarily, for the purpose of manufacturing, distributing, or using any controlled substance...'"

A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital that "the DOJ can confirm receipt of the letter and is ensuring the appropriate personnel within the Department are reviewing it carefully."

President Donald Trump's administration, in a July 2025 executive order, ordered the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to redirect funding from "recipients of Federal housing and homelessness assistance that operate drug injection sites or 'safe consumption sites,' knowingly distribute drug paraphernalia, or permit the use or distribution of illicit drugs on property under their control."

TRUMP’S DC LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS

Malliotakis praised the decision while arguing that the OnPoint facilities fall under that definition.

"Thankfully, President Trump last year signed an executive order prohibiting any federal funds from going to such facilities. There was a $2 million grant that Joe Biden's administration had approved for these facilities in New York, and President Trump's executive order canceled that," she told Fox News Digital.

Malliotakis also introduced a bill in 2025 that would further defund injection centers nationally.

"We don't know who will be president in a few years, so we need that codified in statute. I'm very pleased to see the President took action via executive order to stop $2 million of taxpayer money from going to a heroin shooting gallery, which is an absolutely insane use of taxpayer funds," she told Fox News Digital.

"We're hopeful that under the new Trump administration, we will see these heroin sites finally shut down because what they're doing is enabling addiction," she continued. "It is really unsavory activity that's taking place. You see the quality of life deteriorate, all in full view of the school children attending surrounding community schools," Malliotakis said.

Malliotakis also slammed New York's Democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who visited one of OnPoint's locations in March.

"The new mayor, Zohran Mamdani, did go visit one of these facilities and was praising the work they're doing, which is ludicrous. It's enabling drug addiction instead of helping people who are clearly addicted," she told Fox News Digital.

"These are people addicted to these substances, and instead of helping them fight their addiction and get off drugs, they're literally enabling them and giving them a community center to do it in — when we could use community centers for our youth and our seniors. It's really, really disturbing to see tax dollars go to this" she continued.

"We need long-term treatment. I've been a constant supporter of funding long-term treatment. Unfortunately, here in New York City, when they make a drug-related arrest, it's a quick turnaround — you're in and you're out, even if you're the dealer perpetrating these crimes on people," Malliotakis said.

Fox News Digital contacted the White House, Mamdani's office and OnPoint for further comment.

item.title: John Rich warns Nashville's famed Broadway could go dark as businesses face tax ‘death nail’
item.description: John Rich warns Nashville's Lower Broadway honky-tonks face closure as property tax bills soar, threatening the live music culture that defines Music City.
item.content:encoded:
Country star John Rich is warning that Nashville’s Lower Broadway, the iconic entertainment district famous for its glowing neon signs, packed honky-tonks and live country music, could soon begin going dark.

In a video that Rich shared on Facebook last week, the 52-year-old Big & Rich member sounded the alarm, declaring that "the lights are going out on Broadway" as Nashville businesses struggle under mounting property tax bills.

Speaking to Fox News Digital, Rich, who owns Redneck Riviera Bar & BBQ on Lower Broadway, argued that sharply higher property assessments along with increased taxes have pushed longtime Broadway establishments to a breaking point, which he said threatened not only the businesses themselves but the live music culture that earned Nashville its "Music City" nickname.

"It was a one-two punch," Rich said. "So the first thing he did was they reappraised everybody's property in the county, in the city, and as soon as they got that done, which was an extremely inflated appraisal rate, then they come in and raise the taxes aggressively on top of these extremely inflated appraisals."

COUNTRY STAR JOHN RICH JOINS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ADVOCATING FOR LANDOWNERS' RIGHTS

"And with those two things, what you've done is you've now put a death nail in a vast majority of the businesses," he continued. "It's only a matter of time before you're going to see large percentages of the businesses downtown turning out the lights."

"We've already had three in the past two weeks have to shut down. I'm talking major, major, major places that have been there for decades," Rich added.

Though Rich blamed Nashville Mayor Freddie O’Connell for the overall tax burden, the city's regularly scheduled four-year reappraisal, which took place in 2025, was conducted by the independently elected Davidson County assessor of property.

WATCH: JOHN RICH WARNS TAX ‘ONE-TWO PUNCH’ THREATENS BROADWAY

The 2025 reappraisal resulted in a 45% median increase in property values countywide. Under Tennessee law, the reappraisal itself is revenue-neutral, meaning the tax rate is adjusted so higher property values don't automatically generate additional revenue for local government.

However, O’Connell and the Metro Council subsequently set the Urban Services District tax rate at $2.814 per $100 of assessed value, 26% above the revenue-neutral certified rate, according to the assessor’s office.

The increases were particularly steep on Lower Broadway, where a 400% increase in real estate values was common, according to a report by Axios Nashville. The outlet also reported that many honky-tonk operators rent their buildings and are responsible for the property taxes under their leases, leaving them to shoulder rising tax bills without benefiting from the increased equity in the properties.

Rich pointed to several Lower Broadway establishments while describing what he sees as a broader threat to businesses in the district.

He cited Nashville Underground, which permanently closed in May after roughly eight years in business, and Acme Feed & Seed, whose owner, Tom Morales, has warned it could close amid a steep increase in its property tax bill. Rich also said he has heard Hard Rock Cafe Nashville, a Broadway fixture since 1994, is considering closing, though Fox News Digital has not independently confirmed that claim.

Acme Feed & Seed, in particular, has emerged as a flashpoint in the debate over the rising tax burden. In February, Morales said the popular four-story restaurant, bar and live music venue's annual property tax bill had jumped from $129,000 to nearly $600,000.

Morales told Nashville's NewsChannel 5 that Acme Feed & Seed ended 2025 about $500,000 "in the red," while he and his daughter Lauren Morales later told the Nashville Scene that closure was "imminent" if they could not find a solution to the tax increase.

O’Connell addressed Morales' warnings at the time during an interview with Nashville's Fox 17.

"It’s not up to me whether he keeps that business open," O’Connell told the outlet. "The market evolves. New businesses start even as beloved old businesses close."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

The comments drew criticism, including from Metro Councilmember Jacob Kupin, who told Fox 17 he was "appalled" by the mayor's response. O’Connell’s office later accused the station of selectively editing and misrepresenting his remarks and released a longer version of the exchange.

In the fuller answer, O’Connell said the state comptroller had reviewed downtown valuations and determined they reflected market value. He called Acme's location "an incredibly valuable piece of property" and said it was up to the owner to determine how to capture that value.

Rich argued that Acme’s concerns are far from isolated, pointing to a recent meeting he attended with other Lower Broadway business owners.

"Then we had this meeting with all the business owners down there," Rich told Fox News Digital. "And in that meeting, all the ownership of Broadway was represented down there, and every single person said it's only a matter of time before we literally have to just close the doors because we're running at a deficit."

"We'd have to charge $50 a beer, which you can't do that," he continued. "I mean, there is no business model that exists that allows the businesses down there to stay open."

WATCH: JOHN RICH SAYS NASHVILLE BARS WOULD NEED TO CHARGE ‘$50 A BEER' TO SURVIVE

Rich emphasized that the bar and restaurant operators sounding the alarm include some of the most experienced in the city.

"You're not talking about a bunch of amateurs here," he said. "You're looking at the best of the best, and they can't survive it."

For Rich, however, the bigger concern is what the financial pressure could ultimately mean for Nashville’s identity.

"The bigger story to me is live music in Nashville. I mean, it's called Music City," he said.

Rich described the unique concentration of live music along Broadway, where honky-tonks line both sides of the street and bands perform throughout the day and into the early morning hours.

"You walk down Broadway, the doors are all open to all the honky-tonks, you're hearing music from the right side of your head and the left side of your head for five blocks in a row," Rich said. "There's 60, 70, 80 live music venues in that one concentration. It's the only place like it in the world."

"The French Quarter doesn't have that. Las Vegas doesn't have that. Times Square doesn't have that," he continued. "There's nowhere in America that has what downtown Nashville has when it comes to live music. And it is absolutely under threat."

Rich painted a dire picture of what he fears the entertainment district could eventually look like when Nashville hosts the 2030 Super Bowl.

"Can you imagine when the Super Bowl comes to Nashville here in a few years, and everybody's packed in on Broadway and there's only 30 or 40% of the neon signs that are even still lit up, if you're lucky?" he said. "That's what you're looking at happening. I mean, what a travesty that would be."

Rich, an outspoken conservative and longtime supporter of President Donald Trump, placed much of the blame for the situation on O’Connell, a Democrat, suggesting the mayor's approach to the issue is driven by ideology. However, Rich maintained that concerns among Broadway business owners cross political lines.

"This is not just a bunch of conservatives yelling about it," Rich said. "The group of business owners that I sat with were from both sides of the aisle."

"There's all kinds of things we don't agree on amongst each other," he continued. "But this right here brought unity amongst left and right and middle. It's that bad."

Rich also accused O’Connell of using tax policy to reshape the character of Nashville, offering his own view of the mayor's motivations.

"It is a tactic to tax things out of existence that you don't like and replace them with things that you'd rather have there," Rich said. "Can you imagine the neon signs on Broadway replaced with government buildings and corporate offices? I think that's what he wants."

Fox News Digital has reached out to O’Connell’s office for comment.

The five-time Grammy Award nominee is now calling on Tennessee state leaders to intervene.

Rich said Broadway business owners have appealed to Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton and Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson and urged Gov. Bill Lee to work with lawmakers on a solution. He told Fox News Digital that the governor has the opportunity to become a "honky-tonk hero."

WATCH: JOHN RICH FEARS NASHVILLE’S NEON LIGHTS COULD GO DARK BEFORE SUPER BOWL COMES TO MUSIC CITY

"Governor Lee, who's still here, has an opportunity to do a special session with the Senate, with the House, and come with some solution that, if nothing else, will buy us some time until we can go in and make the more permanent moves," Rich said.

State leaders are considering taking action. Sexton's office confirmed to Axios Nashville on Wednesday that the House speaker has spoken with Lee's office about the issue and that they are "looking at all possible solutions," including the possibility of a special legislative session.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Despite his warnings, Rich said the culture that draws crowds to Broadway has not changed, at least not yet.

"The culture on Broadway hasn't changed at all," he said. "The crowds that come there, the bands that play there, the owners of those businesses, they're the same as they've always been."

"It is all about the music," Rich continued. "It's all about people coming to town to have a good time and look at what some of the most talented people you've ever seen in your life play on these tiny little stages."

item.title: El-Sayed argued against the Second Amendment in unearthed social media videos
item.description: Abdul El-Sayed hid roughly 100 YouTube videos before launching his Michigan Senate campaign, including clips arguing to amend the Second Amendment.
item.content:encoded:
A controversial progressive Democrat who has campaigned with high-profile socialists and is running to be the state's next U.S. senator from Michigan responded after hidden videos on his YouTube channel trashing the Second Amendment resurfaced.

"Abdul respects the Second Amendment, and also believes that access to healthcare is a right," Abdul El-Sayed spokeswoman Roxie Richner told Fox News Digital when reached for comment about comments made in the now-secret videos.

"What if we tweaked the Constitution, amended the amendment, and instead of the right to bear arms, we change it to the right to have health care?" he said in a YouTube video posted on April 6, 2023.

He claimed altruism in the proposal, saying more people would live. In that video, El-Sayed said that stripping Second Amendment rights and implementing a right to healthcare policy would lead to "fewer people dying by gun and more people living because they have healthcare."

MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED DODGES QUESTION ON WHETHER HE STILL SUPPORTS DEFUNDING THE POLICE

YouTube offers a feature to hide videos previously posted publicly without deleting them.

Though the hidden videos can't be viewed, rough transcripts can be found on an internet archive site first revealed by CNN in a Monday report. The outlet reports that El-Sayed hid about 100 videos before launching his Senate campaign.

In one video from May 26, 2022, the transcript of which was viewed by Fox News Digital, El-Sayed made the argument that the Second Amendment does not apply to individual Americans and only applies to a regulated militia. He claimed that the stipulation written in the key constitutional right "couches the entire idea of not infringing on the right to bear arms in the idea of maintaining a well-regulated militia."

He argued against individuals owning firearms, instead suggesting that only designated community-based groups, like police forces, should be issued firearms. Paradoxically, El-Sayed has also argued in favor of defunding the police.

UNEARTHED CLIP EXPOSES MORE ANTI-POLICE RHETORIC AS EL-SAYED GETS GRILLED FOR DELETING SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS

That argument against the Second Amendment was roundly rejected in a famous Supreme Court case from 2008, District of Columbia v. Heller.

"The Second Amendment protects an individual right to possess a firearm unconnected with service in a militia," the nation's highest court decidedly held.

El-Sayed's campaign did not respond when asked which, if any, of his views on the Second Amendment had changed since posting the 2022 and 2023 videos.

Among the many other hidden videos, El-Sayed also raged against President Donald Trump's closed borders policies, argued against the use of fireworks and compared the "ethos" of football to slavery.

The Democrat candidate has campaigned with socialist darling streamer Hasan Piker, known for saying "America deserved 9/11," praising Mao Zedong and Communist China, arguing that capitalists should be murdered in the streets and spewing a litany of antisemitic bile.

The two palled around at a pre-primary election day party earlier this month.

item.title: Three states prepare to execute killers Thursday in same-day event not seen since 2010
item.description: Three men face lethal injection Thursday in Tennessee, Alabama and Oklahoma in a rare same-day execution cluster not seen in the U.S. since 2010.
item.content:encoded:
Three men in three different states are scheduled to be executed by lethal injection on Thursday in an unusual same-day cluster of executions across the U.S.

Tennessee is set to execute Anthony Darrell Hines for the murder of a motel maid, while Alabama plans to put Jeremy Williams to death for raping and killing a 5-year-old girl after paying her mother $2,500 to let the child perform a sexual act. Oklahoma is also scheduled to execute Carlos Cuesta-Rodriguez for killing his girlfriend.

The Associated Press reported that three states last carried out executions on a single day on Jan. 7, 2010, when prisoners were put to death in Louisiana, Ohio and Texas.

TWO FLORIDA INMATES DIE IN RARE DOUBLE EXECUTION AFTER SCOTUS DENIES STAYS

Three executions were also set to happen on the same day in 2018, though only one took place after Alabama officials struggled to place an IV line and Texas granted a reprieve.

Florida executed two men in one day in July, bringing its total number of executions since the beginning of 2025 to 31.

item.title: Man who carried Clinton nuclear 'football' reveals what 'scares the hell out of me' about Air Force One story
item.description: Retired Air Force Lt. Col. Robert Patterson said he suspects a "highly placed" leaker revealed the story of President Donald Trump's Air Force One swap.
item.content:encoded:
A retired Air Force lieutenant colonel who carried the nuclear "football" for former President Bill Clinton says the extraordinary Air Force One shell game departing Ankara, Turkey, last month to protect President Donald Trump from a potential attack was hardly unprecedented.

"It was brilliant," retired Lt. Col. Robert "Buzz" Patterson told Fox News Digital. "I wish I had been a part of it. That's how well done it was."

But Patterson is warning that exposing the vital national security secrets behind such operations could put presidents, military personnel and the White House press corps in danger for years to come.

Patterson served as Clinton's senior military aide for a period of two years and was responsible for the president’s emergency satchel, and in a 20-minute interview Wednesday, he explained how presidential decoys, aircraft swaps and other acts of deception are longstanding tools used to protect the commander in chief, his senior officials and the "privileged" Air Force One press corps.

TRUMP USED CATERING TRUCK, AIR FORCE ONE DECOY TO EVADE IRAN THREAT: REPORT

What alarms him, Patterson said, is not that Trump’s security team used the tactic — including the catering truck sleight of hand he was intimately a part of during the Clinton administration — but that details of how it was done are now spilling into public view.

"I hope that they prosecute this to the fullest," Patterson said. "Whoever leaked that, in my opinion, and having been involved in this, was highly placed in that process."

"There’s only a few people who actually know exactly what’s going down, and that’s by design," he added. "So if somebody leaked it, it was somebody involved in the process, and that scares the hell out of me."

'DECOY' AIR FORCE ONE WAS PROTECTED BY US FIGHTER JETS, OFFICIAL SAYS

His warning comes as Fox News reported Wednesday that the legacy presidential 747 used as a decoy after Trump secretly switched planes in Ankara, Turkey, last month was not sent into the sky unprotected.

A senior Trump administration official told Fox News that U.S. fighter jets protected the aircraft on its flight to the United Kingdom. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were also aboard with members of the traveling press corps, according to the official. Reporters had been instructed to keep their window shades closed.

Patterson said the fighter escort was exactly the sort of protection he would expect in a high-threat environment.

TRUMP SAYS HE'S IRAN'S 'NO. 1' TARGET AS RENEWED CONFLICT RAISES ASSASSINATION FEARS

"Yes, especially into war zones," Patterson said, when asked whether presidential aircraft are customarily escorted by fighter jets in such circumstances.

"We damn sure always do when we’re going to a theater of high threat," he said. "We did it with President Clinton in ’97. And we did it with Trump just a couple weeks ago, and we’ll do it with whoever the next president is."

TRUMP’S SLY PLANE SWITCH RAISES EYEBROWS OVER SAFETY OF PASSENGERS LEFT BEHIND ON BOARD

Trump’s July 8 departure from the NATO summit in Ankara involved a carefully staged deception.

Trump publicly boarded the familiar blue-and-white presidential 747 before being moved out of sight in an airport catering vehicle and transferred to a smaller Air Force C-32A. The legacy 747 then departed for Britain while Trump traveled separately. He later reunited with the presidential aircraft in the United Kingdom before continuing his journey aboard the newer, Qatari-donated 747.

Trump said Tuesday that he was following the direction of the Secret Service and the military.

Patterson said the broader concept of confusing potential attackers about the president’s movements is routine.

WHITE HOUSE PUSHED FOR PROTOCOL TO PRESERVE CORRESPONDENTS' CREDIBILITY AFTER TRUMP'S SECRET PLANE SWITCH

"We use decoys all the time," he said. "We use decoy in the motorcade routes."

"You'll sometimes see the two beasts will switch out under bridges and overpasses. We do the same thing with airplanes, especially in international trips. There's always two Air Force Ones that go. Obviously, one's a decoy and it's also a spare for spare parts in case something happens to the primary.

"So we've been doing it for years.

"It works," he added, "and for people to want to have visibility into actually how it works would be particularly troubling and it would cause reverberations in our American system for years."

SECRET SERVICE AGENT ON JD VANCE'S DETAIL INVESTIGATED FOR ALLEGEDLY LEAKING OPERATIONAL SECURITY INFO

That is why, he argued, demands to expose the mechanics of the latest operation risk doing more damage than the public scrutiny is worth.

Patterson said the protections are intended not merely for Trump, Clinton or any individual president, but to ensure continuity of the presidency itself.

"President Trump's only got two more years," he said. "These programs are going to be in place for the foreseeable future, and they've been in place in our past for quite a while. So it's not just about Trump. These programs exist to protect no matter who the president is and the team around him."

Patterson, who is a conservative and outspoken New York Times bestselling author highly critical of the man he carried the nuclear football for, warned divisive politics against Trump is dangerous for U.S. national security.

TWO YEARS AFTER BUTLER, THREATS AGAINST TRUMP KEEP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT IN SHARP FOCUS

"Like I was with President Clinton — I wasn't a huge President Clinton fan, but they hired me into that position, the White House did — and I swore an oath to the office of the presidency, and I did it," Patterson said. "And I think that the people that are working for President Trump right now, whether they like him or don't like him, or agree with his politics or don't agree with this politics, they have to understand that we're there — the Secret Service guys, the apparatus is there — to protect the human being and the office."

Patterson also revealed that Trump was not the first president he knew of to use an airport catering vehicle as part of a clandestine movement: "As far as I know, President Clinton was the first one to do it."

Decades before Trump was moved between aircraft in Ankara, Patterson said a catering truck was used to discreetly move Clinton aboard a presidential aircraft during an episode that was never publicly reported at the time.

"I won't go into a lot of detail, but, President Clinton was incapable of going up the front steps," he said. "So we used a catering truck to get them onto the back of the airplane, unbeknownst to anybody else that was there except for a few of us. And we never told anybody and nobody ever reported it."

TRUMP HAS BECOME AMERICA'S MOST TARGETED LEADER, FACING THREATS EVERY FEW MONTHS

"And we flew back to D.C. kind of unannounced. And we've done it before. I was on with President Clinton in 1997 when we did the surprise visit to Bosnia. So he went to Bosnia on Christmas Eve to surprise the troops. So we didn't tell anybody then. I was all on that trip the entire way, 36 hours nonstop that day. And we didn't tell anybody, and the press didn't know, and they never complained about it.

"And it was important. We wanted to get President Clinton into a war zone without anybody else knowing about it. And that's kind of what was happening to Trump. They wanted to him out of a potential war zone, without anybody knowing about it.

"We do it all the time. It's safe, it's reliable, and the public does not need to know."

Past presidents have repeatedly used secrecy and deception for travel into dangerous areas. Clinton used decoy aircraft during a 2000 trip to Pakistan, while subsequent presidents have made covert or tightly held trips to Iraq, Afghanistan and Ukraine. The precise circumstances and level of knowledge afforded to traveling reporters have differed between administrations.

Patterson pushed back against criticism that Trump’s operation improperly endangered the reporters and officials who continued aboard the legacy presidential aircraft.

He noted that the aircraft was carrying not only journalists but an Air Force crew and senior government officials — and, as Fox News has now reported, was protected by fighter aircraft.

"We’re not going to put those people at risk either," Patterson said flatly of the Air Force personnel.

He argued that some of the media criticism has lost sight of the wider security apparatus involved in presidential travel.

"A lot of what is being spouted on social media and in our mainstream media is factually incorrect," Patterson said, "and it’s actually troubling because it’s going to endanger not only President Trump, but future presidents to come."

Patterson called efforts to expose the procedures "incredibly dangerous" and "irresponsible."

The danger, he said, extends beyond the president.

"It endangers everybody in the process — Secret Service guys, military aide guys, Air Force guys that are on alert, Army guys that are on alert," Patterson said.

The retired officer said presidential protection plans are deliberately compartmentalized so that very few people know the full operation.

That is what makes the source of the disclosures particularly concerning to him.

Patterson warned there could also be a longer-term cost to revealing too much about presidential deception tactics: Future commanders in chief could lose the ability to make surprise visits to troops or enter high-threat regions at all.

If the tactics become predictable, he argued, planners would have to devise entirely new security procedures.

"If we were to expose everything, we would have to overhaul the entire security apparatus of the United States of America," Patterson said, warning that doing so could put "the presidency and the Cabinet members in incredible danger."

Asked whether overexposing such programs could effectively prevent Trump or future presidents from making some high-risk overseas trips, Patterson agreed.

"That’s correct," he said.

For Patterson, that makes the argument over the Trump flight bigger than one president, one press corps or one flight out of Turkey.

The tactics being publicly dissected today, he warned, may be the same ones needed to save a future president — and everyone traveling with that president — tomorrow.

"We just need to leave them alone," Patterson said.

item.title: BZZR 'cutting out the noise' from sports social media space great for creators, sportscaster Jon Alba says
item.description: Jon Alba explains why BZZR offers sports content creators a virtual sports bar free from AI garbage, engagement bait and vitriol on social media.
item.content:encoded:
Social media can be a tricky place.

If you fire off the wrong hot take, you could subject yourself to endless notifications for messages that might make you lose some sleep. BZZR, a social media platform dedicated solely to sports content, is hoping to change that.

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON FOX NEWS DIGITAL

Jon Alba, an Emmy Award-winning sportscaster who co-hosts "The Extreme Life of Matt Hardy" with the legendary professional wrestler, told Fox News Digital he believed that there was a space missing for sports fans to connect online without the hate and vitriol. He said it’s what makes BZZR the place to be for those who have cemented themselves as reputable content creators and those looking to get reps in.

"I have always felt like there was a spot in the sports media space that was unoccupied where a virtual sports bar could meet people who wanted to engage in that space specifically," he said. "When I was 15 years old, back in the early days of podcasting, podcasting didn't even exist. It was like online sports talk radio. There was a platform called YouCaster, and it was essentially a bunch of sports fans, wannabe sports broadcasters, creating content and congregating around each other's content. And the platform didn't last very long, but it was such a great idea.

"And now in the age of access for all of these creators to have a space that is dedicated to solely creating instantaneous, engaging sports content and cutting out the noise, I think that's awesome for the space, and it's a great way for anyone to get an opportunity to get reps and get better at creating content in the sports space. So, I think it's a great arena for that."

BZZR has made it a point to block out the noise and stick solely to sports, and it’s what drew Alba to the platform. The social media platform has partnered with the Texas Rangers, John Bradshaw Layfield, MVP, Dwayne Swayze and Kayla Becker — to name a few.

"And I think the advantage of a place like BZZR is that you have people on the platform who are there for the right reason, who want to create good, engaging content that furthers conversation that gets them better at creating sports content and creates a space that people actually want to talk about sports in, as silly as it sounds.

"I don't think we have that many of them right now that do so in a way that has integrity and is genuinely fun to sort through. So that's why I've really gone behind the idea of BZZR and I think it's cool to see that it has grown in a short period of time."

Hardy agreed that the concept of having a place solely for sports was a good idea.
